item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk Morning Brief for July 31, 2026
item.description: Slower U.S. growth, an immigration detention setback for the White House, Medicare drug-cost fallout, and Seattle’s police leadership shakeup lead the national brief before Debt Desk turns to Friday’s verified curve, steady SOFR, active CMBS and agency issuance, fresh multifamily financings, and the next rate signal to watch on July 31, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
It is Friday, July 31st, and this is Debt Desk.

National

Let’s start with the morning brief, and this Friday the national picture looks like a reminder that the market is still being forced to balance two competing realities at the same time. On one side, the economy is still moving. On the other, the policy, legal and cost backdrop around that economy keeps getting more complicated.

The biggest headline this morning is the new growth read. The Associated Press reported Thursday that the U.S. economy expanded at a 1.5 percent annual pace in the second quarter, down from 2.1 percent in the first quarter and below expectations. That is not a recession print, and it is not even a collapse story, but it is a slowdown story. What makes it more interesting is that the softer headline does not really tell you the whole thing fell apart underneath. Consumer spending still grew at a 3.2 percent annual rate, which says households are still participating even with a lot of frustration around prices. The problem is that inflation is still sticky enough to keep pressure on the Federal Reserve, with AP reporting that the PCE index rose 3.7 percent from a year earlier and core PCE came in at 3.3 percent. So the takeaway is not simply that growth cooled. It is that growth cooled without giving the country a clean inflation victory. For markets, that is the kind of mix that keeps the rate conversation unsettled, because softer growth alone is not enough if price pressure is still running above target.

The second story is immigration and the courts, where AP reported Thursday that the Ninth Circuit rejected the Trump administration’s attempt to expand mandatory detention for immigrants arrested inside the United States without giving them a chance to seek bond. The decision deepens the circuit split, because several appeals courts have now rejected the administration’s reading while others have backed it. That matters beyond immigration politics. It is one more sign that a wide set of executive-branch priorities are still moving through the courts in a fragmented way, which keeps policy risk elevated even when the White House feels politically committed to a direction. For businesses, local governments and legal advisers, that means the compliance environment remains uneven. A policy can be aggressively pursued in Washington and still remain operationally unsettled across the country.

The third story gets right back to household costs. AP reported Thursday that the Trump administration is ending the temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program that was helping hold down prescription-drug premiums for seniors. Officials insist the direct hit to beneficiaries should be limited, but the timing is politically sensitive because older voters are highly engaged, cost of living remains a top concern, and every additional monthly bill matters much more when households already feel squeezed. This is one of those stories where the dollar impact may not be fully visible yet, but the political impact starts immediately because the signal is clear. Washington is willing to remove a visible consumer cushion at a time when voters are still telling pollsters they do not feel much relief.

The fourth story is out of Seattle, where AP reported Thursday that Police Chief Shon Barnes resigned after heavy criticism of the city’s response and communications after last weekend’s deadly shooting at the Bite of Seattle festival. The local facts matter, but the broader read-through matters too. Public trust is now being tested not only on crime itself but on response speed, clarity and competence in the hours after a major incident. That is increasingly a national governance theme. People are judging institutions less by what they promise in advance and more by whether they can communicate clearly during pressure events. For cities trying to sustain tourism, downtown activity and major event calendars, that becomes an economic story as well as a public-safety story.

So that is the national setup this morning. Growth is slowing, but not enough to make inflation someone else’s problem. The courts are still actively redrawing the boundaries of federal policy. Healthcare affordability is back in focus for older Americans. And city leadership, especially around public safety, remains under direct scrutiny. That is the backdrop as we turn to debt.

Debt Desk

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk, where the first job this morning is to anchor everything to the verified market prints.

Using the local checker tied to the official Treasury table and the New York Fed SOFR feed, the latest available Treasury close is Thursday, July 30. The curve closed at 4.23 percent on the 2-year, 4.38 percent on the 5-year, 4.68 percent on the 10-year and 5.21 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.65 percent for July 29.

That is not a dramatic move from the prior day, but it keeps the same message intact. The long end is still doing enough work to make duration expensive, even though front-end funding costs are no longer the singular problem they were when floating debt felt punishing every single day. The gap from the 2-year to the 10-year is about 45 basis points, and the jump from the 2-year to the 30-year is just under a full point. In practical terms, borrowers are still paying up for certainty. If you are trying to place longer fixed-rate debt, especially on a deal that is not pristine, the curve is not giving you much charity. At the same time, SOFR holding in the mid-3s means bridge structures remain workable for business plans that still need time. So the rate backdrop continues to sort borrowers rather than shut the market. Stabilized assets can still make sense with permanent debt. Transitional assets can still make sense with floating-rate capital. But nobody is getting a free option from the curve.

The second major point is that securitized markets continue to backstop that message. CREFC’s July 28 CRE Securitized Debt Update said year-to-date 2026 private-label CMBS and CRE CLO issuance reached $103.9 billion, up 21 percent from the same point last year, while spreads mostly held steady. That is important because it tells you the market is still capable of digesting supply even with the macro backdrop unsettled. It is not a euphoric market, but it is a functioning market, and in commercial real estate debt that distinction matters a lot. When issuance is moving and spreads are not lurching wider, lenders and borrowers both gain a little more confidence that execution windows are real.

The third point is that loan performance data still says the system is carrying stress even while new money is flowing. CREFC’s June 2026 Monthly CMBS Loan Performance Report, released July 28, showed overall CMBS delinquency falling 20 basis points to 7.35 percent, but special servicing rising 34 basis points to 11.20 percent. That combination is the part worth paying attention to. The market is creating liquidity faster than it is fully resolving legacy problems. Some loans are curing, some are refinancing, and some are being transferred into workouts before they become straightforward defaults. That is why the market can feel healthier on the issuance side than it does on the asset-management side. If you are a borrower, that means lenders may be open for business while still under intense internal pressure on underwriting, reserves and structure.

That plays directly into execution tone across lender buckets. Banks are lending, but mostly where the relationship matters, the cash flow is believable and the underwriting can survive a tougher committee conversation. Life companies are still competitive for lower-leverage, higher-quality multifamily and industrial stories, but the elevated long end keeps them disciplined on proceeds. CMBS remains a live lane for assets that fit securitization logic, usually scale, durable occupancy and sponsorship that needs little explaining. Debt funds still have the widest aperture for complexity, especially when timing, structure, lease-up or recapitalization risk matters more than simple coupon. Northmarq’s current rates page and its 2026 debt outlook both support that framing. The market has capital, but deployment remains selective and strategy still matters as much as pricing.

Multifamily continues to be the strongest proof point.

One of the fresher multifamily financing stories came Thursday from Multi-Housing News, which reported that Baron Property Group refinanced and recapitalized Metro Parc in Hialeah, Florida, with a $226.5 million package from Yellowstone Real Estate and Madison Realty Capital while lease-up continues. The property is nearly 50 percent leased, so this is not a sleepy stabilized refinance. It is a live example of debt fund and alternative-capital execution still stepping into transitional multifamily where the scale is meaningful and the lease-up story is clear enough to underwrite.

The affordable lane is active too. Multi-Housing News reported July 29 that a Gilbane-led venture capitalized Chapanoke, a $93 million affordable housing project in Raleigh, with Greystone supplying a construction loan and Citi providing permanent debt alongside subordinate public financing from Wake County and the city. That is a useful deal to keep in mind because it shows how the multifamily market is still getting transactions closed through stacked capital structures when there is a clear public-policy angle and enough institutional support around the deal.

Another good read-through came from Fort Lauderdale, where Multi-Housing News reported July 28 that Affiliated Development secured a $74 million construction loan from Pacific Life for The Cove, a 376-unit mixed-income project with more than half the units reserved for workforce housing. That one matters for two reasons. First, it shows life company capital still willing to support multifamily construction when the borrower, market and affordability story line up. Second, it reinforces a theme we have been watching for weeks now: workforce and mixed-income angles continue to improve the conversation around execution even when lenders are otherwise staying selective.

Agency liquidity is still one of the clearest supports underneath the apartment market. CREFC’s same July 28 update showed $5.3 billion of agency CMBS issuance for the week, including Fannie DUS, Freddie Multi-PC, Freddie K and Ginnie executions, with year-to-date agency issuance running 23 percent above last year. That tells you the agency lane remains deep and dependable, especially compared with the more case-by-case tone in some bank and life company channels. For borrowers who can fit that box, agencies are still giving the market its cleanest permanent-debt option.

On the CMBS side of multifamily specifically, the tone is a little more mixed. Multi-Housing News, citing Trepp data on July 28, noted multifamily CMBS delinquency moved up to 7.71 percent, driven in part by a couple of larger newly delinquent loans. That does not overturn the broader liquidity story, but it does reinforce the point that apartments are not immune from maturity pressure, lease-up risk or financing mismatch. Multifamily is the strongest debt story in the market right now, not a perfect one.

HUD and FHA are relatively quiet this morning. As of today’s check, HUD’s multifamily memos page still shows only a limited set of 2026 multifamily notices, and the main FHA mortgagee-letter page shows recent single-family oriented updates rather than a fresh multifamily catalyst. So the practical reading for today is simple: FHA remains a viable lane where leverage, amortization and mission fit justify the process, but there is no new Washington policy headline resetting that execution channel this morning.

The concise market snapshot for Friday is this. The verified July 30 Treasury curve is 4.23 on the 2-year, 4.38 on the 5-year, 4.68 on the 10-year and 5.21 on the 30-year. SOFR is 3.65 on the latest official print for July 29. CMBS and CRE CLO issuance remain active. Agency multifamily execution is still running ahead of last year. Multifamily deal flow is getting done across affordable, mixed-income and lease-up situations. But lender selectivity remains very real, especially when term risk and business-plan risk show up together.

One thing to watch today is whether the next macro read pushes the long end materially away from this 5.2 percent handle on the 30-year. If the long bond backs up again, expect life company and fixed-rate executions to stay cautious and for more borrowers to lean on shorter bridge structures or debt funds. If the long end stabilizes, the market may squeeze a few more permanent-debt closings through before August gets fully underway.

The takeaway for this Friday morning is that the market is still open, but the burden of proof remains high. Nationally, the economy is slowing without fully cooling inflation, the courts are still reshaping policy implementation, and household-cost politics are still very much alive. In Debt Desk, the curve continues to charge for duration, SOFR is no longer the whole problem, securitized markets are functioning, agencies remain a stabilizer, and multifamily keeps attracting the broadest lender interest. Capital is there. Conviction still has to be earned.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk Morning Brief for July 30, 2026
item.description: The Fed’s split-rate decision, a renewed Fauci flashpoint, an AI free-speech case in Minnesota, and a major Dulles overhaul lead the national brief before Debt Desk turns to Thursday’s verified curve, a steeper long end, fresh securitized issuance, multifamily financing activity, agency execution, and the next catalyst to watch on July 30, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
It is Thursday, July 30th, and this is Debt Desk.

National

Let’s start with the morning brief, because the national picture this Thursday feels unusually tied together by one shared theme: institutions are making bigger bets, bigger threats and bigger policy calls, and markets have to price the follow-through.

The first story is the Federal Reserve, because it set the tone for everything else that follows. The Associated Press reported Wednesday that the Fed left its key rate unchanged, but the headline was not just the hold. It was the three dissents. That matters because a split decision tells you the committee is not settling into a comfortable waiting pattern. It is still arguing about whether inflation risk, energy pressure and broader policy uncertainty are strong enough to justify tighter conditions later this year. For borrowers, lenders and anyone trying to time a refinancing window, that kind of internal division matters almost as much as the rate decision itself. It means the path ahead is still live. The market got no clean all-clear on cuts, no strong new tightening signal, and no reason to assume the next move is easy to forecast. In other words, the Fed bought time, but it did not buy certainty.

The second story is Washington’s latest return to the pandemic-era political fights. AP reported Wednesday that Anthony Fauci repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment in a Republican-led Senate hearing and that Senator Rand Paul plans to move a contempt vote next week. That is obviously a political and legal story first, but it also says something broader about the operating environment in the United States right now. Issues that many businesses assumed were fading into the rearview mirror are still fully alive in congressional oversight, media coverage and voter mobilization. The practical takeaway is that the pandemic is still not just a historical event. It remains an active fault line in politics, public trust and regulatory rhetoric, and those fault lines can keep resurfacing in ways that affect health policy, university research funding and the tone of the 2026 elections.

The third story is out of Minnesota, where AP reported that Elon Musk’s xAI sued the state over its new law banning AI-generated nudification tools. On the surface, that sounds like a tech-law fight. In reality, it is a test case for how aggressively states can regulate generative AI before federal rules catch up. That matters well beyond one lawsuit. If states move first and courts allow a wide patchwork of rules, companies will have to manage product compliance, content moderation and liability state by state. If courts push back, the pressure moves back to Congress and federal agencies. Either way, the market is learning that AI is no longer just a growth story. It is now a policy story, a litigation story and a compliance-cost story.

The fourth story is more concrete, literally. AP reported Wednesday that President Trump announced a $22.5 billion modernization plan for Washington Dulles International Airport. The headline item is replacing the long-disliked people movers, but the bigger takeaway is that the project is meant to rework passenger flow, add new concourses and push a large bond-financed infrastructure plan forward around one of the country’s most important gateway airports. For real estate, transportation and municipal-credit watchers, that is not just a ribbon-cutting story. It points to where capital spending is still politically legible: large visible projects with a clear user base, regional prestige value and a funding stack that can be tied to traffic, fees and long-term growth.

So the national setup this morning is pretty straightforward. The Fed held steady but showed real division. Fauci’s hearing reopened one of the country’s deepest political arguments. xAI’s lawsuit put AI regulation squarely into the courts. And Dulles became a reminder that very large infrastructure spending is still on the table when the politics line up. That is the backdrop as we turn to debt.

Debt Desk

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk.

The first anchor this morning is the verified rates picture, and the tone is different from yesterday because we now have the post-Fed Treasury close. Using the local market-data checker tied to official Treasury and New York Fed sources, the latest available Treasury close is Wednesday, July 29. That leaves us with 4.22 percent on the 2-year, 4.37 percent on the 5-year, 4.67 percent on the 10-year and 5.20 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.65 percent for July 28.

That curve is worth slowing down on. The short end eased, but the long end stayed elevated enough to keep the financing conversation very asset-specific. The spread from the 2-year to the 10-year is now about 45 basis points, and from the 2-year to the 30-year it is close to a full point. That means the market is not paying borrowers to wait for duration. If anything, it is still charging for conviction. A borrower looking at five-year bank paper, a life company quote, or a longer fixed-rate execution is still facing a real cost for pushing term. At the same time, SOFR in the mid-3s means floating-rate carry is no longer at emergency levels. So this is not a frozen market. It is a sorting market. Stable cash flow can still justify term debt. Transitional business plans can still make sense with floating-rate structures. But the old assumption that everyone should automatically push long and lock is still not back.

The second thing to notice is that securitized debt is still moving, and that is a useful signal when people talk as if commercial real estate finance is purely a distress story. CREFC’s July 28 securitized debt update said year-to-date 2026 private-label CMBS and CRE CLO issuance has reached $103.9 billion, up 21 percent from the same period a year ago. Conduit AAA spreads were unchanged at plus 70, A-S at plus 100, and CRE CLO AAA spreads held at plus 130 to plus 135. That is not a euphoric tape, but it is a functioning one. Investors are still funding clean structures, and the spread behavior says buyers are asking for discipline, not fleeing the sector.

The composition of that issuance matters too. In the same CREFC update, one of the highlighted deals was KELR 2026-MF, a $718.5 million SASB backed by a floating-rate, interest-only refinance of 13 multifamily properties across Utah, Nevada and Arizona. Another was a large managed CRE CLO with collateral that was more than 50 percent multifamily. Those details matter because they show where volume can still clear. Multifamily is still the easiest story to securitize, especially when occupancy is strong and the property story is legible in one slide.

Agency paper is reinforcing that same point. CREFC said agency CMBS issuance totaled $5.3 billion last week, including $2.5 billion of Fannie DUS, $1.2 billion in Freddie Multi-PCs, a $1 billion Freddie K transaction and roughly $451 million of Ginnie execution. Year to date, agency issuance is running 23 percent above the same point last year. That is one of the clearest liquidity signals in the market right now. Multifamily borrowers still have a deep agency lane, and that lane remains more dependable than most other permanent debt channels.

That does not mean the stress is gone. Quite the opposite. CREFC’s June 2026 CMBS loan-performance report, released July 28, showed overall CMBS delinquency falling 20 basis points to 7.35 percent, but special servicing rising 34 basis points to 11.20 percent. That pairing is the key story. Delinquencies can improve while special servicing rises when maturing loans are being pushed into workout territory before formal default. In plain English, some loans are getting resolved, but the refinance wall is still pushing fresh volume into the system. So if you are looking for the cleanest summary of the market, it is this: liquidity is back faster than resolution.

That is why execution tone still differs meaningfully by lender bucket. Banks are in the market for relationship business and cleaner stabilized assets, but they still care about deposits, sponsor quality and low-drama underwriting. Life companies remain competitive, particularly on lower-leverage multifamily and industrial stories, but they are not stretching just because Treasury volatility briefly calms down. CMBS remains open for assets that can stand up to securitization logic, which usually means scale, durable occupancy and sponsorship that needs little explanation. Debt funds are still the most useful outlet for complexity, especially where timing, lease-up, recapitalization or structure matters more than coupon.

Northmarq’s current rates and market commentary continue to support that read. Their live rates page still shows Treasury and SOFR benchmarks that keep all-in borrowing costs manageable for strong multifamily deals, while their 2026 debt-market outlook says banks are active on stabilized assets, life company allocations are increasing, agency execution remains competitive and underwriting discipline is still intact. That lines up with what the tape is showing in actual transactions: capital is available, but it is not forgiving.

On fresh deal flow, the multifamily lane continues to do the heaviest lifting. Multi-Housing News reported on July 29 that a Gilbane-led joint venture capitalized a $93 million affordable housing project in Raleigh, with Greystone providing the construction loan and Citi supplying permanent debt alongside public subordinate financing. That matters because it is a reminder that affordable housing still assembles capital stacks that would be much harder to replicate in other property types.

The day before, Multi-Housing News reported that Affiliated Development landed a $74 million construction loan for a Fort Lauderdale mixed-income project, with more than half the units reserved for workforce housing. That is another useful read-through for the market. Capital is still willing to support multifamily development when the affordability story, local demand picture and capital stack are aligned well enough to survive today’s higher-for-longer underwriting.

The agency side added its own process story this week. Fannie Mae’s Lender Letter 26-06, published July 28, updated multifamily loan documents that may be used immediately and become mandatory for qualifying commitments on or after September 8. That is not a headline most borrowers will see, but it matters to anyone trying to close in late summer. When document packages change, timing friction can show up quickly in the final stretch of a deal, especially for borrowers who assume the agency lane is always smooth just because it is open.

Freddie Mac activity remains relevant through issuance as well. The latest agency totals show Freddie still very present in the market through Multi-PC and K executions, and that matters because it keeps a meaningful benchmark for apartment borrowers who need certainty of execution more than they need the absolute tightest theoretical coupon.

HUD and FHA are quieter this morning, and that is worth stating plainly. I did not find a material new multifamily HUD memo or FHA policy bulletin published in the last 24 hours. The practical read is that the FHA lane is still available, but it is not being reset by a new policy catalyst today. That usually means borrowers will keep using FHA where leverage, amortization and mission fit justify the extra process, rather than because of a fresh Washington-driven tailwind.

The concise market snapshot this morning is this. The latest verified Treasury curve is 4.22 percent on the 2-year, 4.37 percent on the 5-year, 4.67 percent on the 10-year and 5.20 percent on the 30-year. SOFR is 3.65 percent for July 28 on the latest official print. Private-label and CRE CLO issuance remains healthy. CMBS spreads are steady enough to support execution. Agency issuance is still strong. Multifamily remains the cleanest debt story in the market. And the gap between headline liquidity and actual underwriting tolerance is still where most deals live or die.

One thing to watch today is whether the next round of macro data reinforces or challenges the post-Fed rates move. If growth or inflation data push the long end higher from here, borrowers who were hoping for a cleaner permanent-debt window may lean harder on bridge lenders and debt funds again. If the long end settles or rallies, expect more apartment owners to test life company, agency and securitized takeout options before summer ends.

The takeaway for this Thursday morning is that the market is open, but it is still asking for proof. Nationally, the news flow is reminding everyone that policy risk, litigation risk and infrastructure politics are all back in the foreground. In Debt Desk, the curve is still making duration expensive, SOFR is no longer the whole problem, securitized markets are functioning, agencies are active, and multifamily keeps attracting the broadest lender interest. The deals are getting done. They are just getting done in a market that still rewards clarity far more than optimism.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk Morning Brief for July 29, 2026
item.description: A deeper Seattle shooting investigation, tornado cleanup in Wisconsin, Senate action on Russia sanctions, and a new anti-China spending push lead the national brief before Debt Desk turns to Wednesday’s verified curve, steady securitized spreads, fresh multifamily financings, agency process changes, a quiet HUD lane, and one thing to watch on July 29, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
It is Wednesday, July 29th, and this is Debt Desk.

National

Let’s start with the morning brief, because the national setup this Wednesday is a mix of public safety, weather disruption, geopolitics and Washington policy all feeding into the same broader question for markets and operators: how much fresh uncertainty is building into day-to-day decision making?

The Seattle festival shooting remains on the board this morning because the story took a meaningful turn again in the last 24 hours. The Associated Press reported Tuesday that the 15-year-old arrested after the gunfire near Seattle’s Space Needle was carrying a ghost gun with an extended magazine, and police now say there were at least three suspects involved. Investigators recovered multiple weapons and shell casings from different calibers, which tells you this is moving beyond a narrow arrest update and into a larger security and enforcement story. For local governments and event operators, that matters. Cities have spent the last few years trying to rebuild confidence in downtown foot traffic, public events and leisure spending. When a high-profile summer festival turns into a multi-shooter investigation, it raises fresh questions about security posture, staffing and how quickly a city can lose momentum in the middle of peak seasonal activity.

The second story is out of Wisconsin, where severe weather damage is now shifting from the immediate storm headline into recovery and damage assessment. AP reported Tuesday that crews were searching damaged buildings in Appleton and surrounding areas after a powerful tornado tore through the region. Early reports suggested that the time of day may have helped limit casualties, but the physical damage was widespread enough that officials were still checking structures and clearing debris. This matters beyond the weather map. Tornado and storm events do not just create insured losses. They hit distribution, small business continuity, labor availability, temporary housing demand and municipal response budgets all at once. In a rate-sensitive environment, every added repair bill and every insurance repricing cycle eventually shows up somewhere in capital stacks and underwriting assumptions.

The third national story is from Washington, where the Senate took a first procedural step on a Russia sanctions package while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy watched from the Senate gallery. AP reported that senators backed the measure 86 to 12 in a bipartisan procedural vote tied closely to the late Lindsey Graham’s final legislative push. The geopolitical implications matter on their own, but there is also a straightforward market read here. A broader sanctions push can affect energy, shipping, global trade flows and risk sentiment even before any final legislative text reaches the finish line. It is another reminder that macro risk is still being driven as much by foreign policy headlines as by economic data.

The fourth story is a quieter but still important Washington development. AP reported Tuesday that the administration is preparing a major increase in anti-China spending around the world, including a $175.8 million undersea cable initiative in the Caribbean and Central America and the possibility of hundreds of millions more across the Western Hemisphere, Africa and Asia. The framing is strategic competition, but the economic angle is hard to miss. Undersea cables, ports, cyber infrastructure and critical minerals are not abstract national-security concepts anymore. They are capital allocation decisions with real implications for construction, equipment demand, sovereign relationships and the supply chain map that U.S. companies and lenders have to price.

So the national frame this morning looks like this: the Seattle shooting has become a bigger policing and public-space story as the weapons picture sharpens; Wisconsin is moving from storm warning to cleanup and cost counting; the Senate has opened a new sanctions chapter tied to Russia and Ukraine; and Washington is signaling that strategic competition with China will keep showing up in hard-dollar spending decisions. That is the backdrop before we get to debt and rates.

Debt Desk

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk.

The first anchor this morning is rates, and the figures are verified through the local market-data checker using official Treasury and New York Fed sources. The latest available Treasury close is Tuesday, July 28. That leaves us with 4.26 percent on the 2-year, 4.35 percent on the 5-year, 4.61 percent on the 10-year, and 5.09 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.64 percent for July 27, with reported volume just under $3 trillion.

That curve matters because it is giving borrowers a little more room than the market was offering a few sessions ago, but not enough to call this an easy lock environment. The 10-year in the low 4.6s and the 30-year a touch above 5 still leave permanent debt expensive by post-pandemic standards, while SOFR in the mid-3s keeps floating-rate carry from feeling truly cheap. The curve from 2s to 30s is still positively sloped, and that is the practical message for borrowers this morning. Short money is no longer punitive in the way it felt when overnight benchmarks were closer to peak levels, but longer-duration money still asks for conviction. If you are borrowing against a stable cash-flow story, fixed-rate executions can work. If you are still leasing up, still renovating or still solving a refinance gap, floating debt and shorter-duration structures remain part of the conversation for a reason.

The next thing to notice is that securitized issuance is still moving, and spreads are not telling a panic story. The CRE Finance Council’s July 28 securitized debt update said year-to-date 2026 private-label CMBS and CRE CLO issuance has reached $103.9 billion, up 21 percent from the same point last year. In that same update, conduit AAA spreads were unchanged at plus 70, and CRE CLO AAA spreads were unchanged at roughly plus 130 to plus 135 depending on structure. That is not a loose market, but it is a functioning one. The bigger takeaway is that investors are still providing capital when structures are familiar, collateral is understandable and sponsorship is credible.

Agency issuance is adding to that message. CREFC said agency CMBS issuance totaled $5.3 billion last week, including $2.5 billion in Fannie DUS, $1.2 billion in Freddie Multi-PCs, a $1 billion Freddie K transaction and about $451 million in Ginnie execution. Agency issuance for the year is running 23 percent above the same period in 2025. That is a strong signal that multifamily liquidity is not theoretical. It is active, visible and still one of the deepest channels in the market.

At the same time, the legacy stress in CMBS has not disappeared. CREFC’s June 2026 loan performance update shows overall conduit and SASB CMBS delinquency at 7.35 percent, down 20 basis points from the prior month, while special servicing climbed to 11.20 percent. That combination is worth paying attention to. Delinquencies can improve while special servicing rises if borrowers are still struggling with maturities and extensions before loans formally default. In other words, some headline distress metrics are getting better, but the refinancing wall is still very real. That is why conduit execution is open, but still selective.

The freshest deal flow keeps pointing to the same conclusion: lenders still want apartments, and they still want stories they can explain quickly. Commercial Real Estate Direct reported Tuesday that Arbor Realty Trust provided $146.24 million of Fannie Mae financing on Manhattan apartments at 7 Dey Street. Multi-Housing News also reported Tuesday that Affiliated Development landed a $74 million construction loan from Pacific Life Insurance Company for a 376-unit mixed-income project in Fort Lauderdale, while a PGIM and Dinerstein venture received an $81 million refinancing from Mesa West Capital on a 330-unit Denver-area property. Those three deals sit in different lanes, but together they say a lot. Agency money is still available for core apartment execution. Life companies will step in on the right workforce and mixed-income construction story. Debt funds are still active where refinance or transitional needs call for more flexibility.

That lines up cleanly with the live pricing tone from Northmarq’s July 28 rate sheet. Fannie and Freddie conventional multifamily quotes are still broadly in the mid-5s to low-6s depending on leverage and structure. Life company multifamily quotes are still competitive on high-quality lower-leverage business, but they remain disciplined and selective. CMBS is generally wider, with rate indications running well above agency executions. FHA is still relevant, especially on 223(f) and 221(d)(4) structures, but it remains a process-heavy option that borrowers use when leverage, amortization or mission fit justify the extra time. So the stack this morning looks familiar: banks are back in the market for strong relationships and cleaner stories, life companies are active but choosy, CMBS is working where collateral and sponsorship are obvious, and debt funds remain the most practical solution set for complexity, speed and transitional business plans.

On the multifamily capital-markets side, there are two agency process points worth carrying forward because they are still shaping execution right now. Fannie Mae posted Lender Letter 26-06 on July 28, updating loan documents that can be used immediately and become mandatory for qualifying loans with commitment dates on or after September 8. That sounds technical, but these procedural changes matter because many near-term deals sit right at the boundary between easy standardization and slow documentation drift. On the Freddie side, the platform’s recent push toward more transparent Multi-PC pricing is still relevant because investors and lenders are watching securitization execution more closely as rates move around and spread discipline holds.

HUD and FHA are quieter this morning, and that is useful information by itself. I did not find a new HUD multifamily memo or FHA multifamily policy development in the last 24 hours on the official pages reviewed for this run. So the practical read is that the FHA lane remains operational rather than catalytic. Borrowers who need its proceeds, term or affordability fit can still use it, but there is no fresh policy change today that resets execution assumptions.

The concise market snapshot this morning is straightforward. The latest verified Treasury curve is 4.26 on the 2-year, 4.35 on the 5-year, 4.61 on the 10-year and 5.09 on the 30-year. SOFR is 3.64 on the latest official print. Securitized issuance is healthy, agency issuance is strong, multifamily still attracts the deepest bid, and execution remains available across the stack as long as the story is clear and the structure matches the business plan.

One thing to watch today is the Federal Reserve. The meeting concludes later on Wednesday, July 29, and even if the Fed does exactly what the market expects on the policy rate, the statement, press conference and market reaction could still move the long end enough to change borrower behavior immediately. If the 10-year stays in this lower 4.6 range or drifts softer, more owners may decide the permanent debt window is good enough to stop waiting. If the long end backs up again, expect bridge lenders, debt funds and creative refinance structures to stay busy well into August.

The takeaway for this Wednesday morning is that the market is not frozen, but it is still highly selective. Nationally, the news flow is reminding everyone that public safety, weather, geopolitics and strategic competition can all move straight into economic decision making. In Debt Desk, the curve is a little friendlier than it was at the highs, securitized spreads are holding together, agencies continue to do real volume, and multifamily remains the asset class with the clearest path to execution. But capital is still demanding clarity. If borrowers want the best terms in this market, they still need clean collateral, realistic leverage and a story lenders can defend in one meeting.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk Morning Brief for July 28, 2026
item.description: A gang-linked turn in the Seattle festival shooting, a major Oregon wildfire shutdown, tariff fallout, and cooling oil prices lead the national brief before Debt Desk turns to Tuesday’s verified curve, multifamily-heavy CRE CLO issuance, apartment refinance demand, selective CMBS windows, agency execution and one thing to watch for Tuesday, July 28, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
It is Tuesday, July 28th, and this is Debt Desk.

National

Let’s start with the morning brief, because the national setup this Tuesday is a mix of public-safety fallout, climate disruption hitting transportation infrastructure, trade policy that is still rippling through pricing decisions, and an energy market that is trying to cool off without giving anyone much confidence that the pressure is really gone.

The first story to watch this morning is the Seattle festival shooting, and the new detail matters. The Associated Press reported today that investigators now believe there were at least three shooters in the gunfire near the Space Needle during the Bite of Seattle festival, and that the violence may have been gang-related. A 15-year-old suspect is in custody, one 19-year-old suspect was among the dead, and police are still looking for at least one more person. This is no longer just a headline about a tragic public event. It is becoming a broader story about downtown security, event operations and how quickly a city’s recovery narrative can get shaken when violence erupts at a signature gathering. For cities that are still leaning on festivals, sports, restaurants and street-level activity to drive foot traffic, this kind of story lands far beyond one block in Seattle.

The second headline is from Oregon, where the wildfire story has moved from regional concern to major transport disruption. AP reported today that a fast-moving fire in eastern Oregon forced the closure of about 70 miles of Interstate 84, one of the key east-west freight routes in that part of the country, while Huntington was under a Level 3 evacuation order. The fire was still uncontained, weather conditions were working against crews, and smoke was limiting some air support. That matters well beyond the local emergency response. When a major interstate closes, even temporarily, it affects trucking schedules, agricultural movement, insurance assumptions and the way businesses think about resilience in fire-prone corridors. It is a reminder that climate risk is not some separate category from economic risk anymore. It increasingly shows up as direct operating friction.

The third story is trade, where the headline is no longer just that tariffs were announced, but that the legal and political rationale is becoming part of the story. AP reported yesterday that the administration’s new double-digit tariffs on imports from more than 60 countries are being framed as a forced-labor crackdown, while critics see them as an end run around Congress and a way to preserve a broad tariff regime after earlier setbacks. That distinction matters because businesses can adjust to almost any rule if they trust the rule will hold. What is harder to price is a policy environment where the legal foundation itself is part of the dispute. Importers, manufacturers and lenders are all watching the same question now: are these tariffs the new baseline, or just the latest stop in a rolling policy fight that keeps changing the cost map?

The fourth story is the energy market, which finally gave consumers a little relief but not much certainty. AP reported yesterday that oil prices fell sharply after the United States and Iran paused attacks, with Brent dropping back into the mid-80s after running above $100 last week. That is important because the move lower came after a run-up that already pushed the national average gasoline price to about $4.11 a gallon. In other words, the futures market may be calming faster than household budgets. For borrowers, builders and property owners, that matters because fuel costs feed into freight, materials, payroll pressure and inflation expectations. Even if the panic bid in crude has come off, the damage to rate expectations does not disappear overnight.

So that is the national frame for Tuesday, July 28. Seattle’s festival shooting has become a deeper public-safety story as the suspect picture widens. Oregon’s wildfire emergency is now disrupting a major interstate corridor. The administration’s tariff push is still generating uncertainty not just because of the duties themselves, but because of the legal argument underneath them. And oil has backed off, but only after reminding the market how quickly geopolitics can move straight into consumer prices. That is the backdrop coming into Debt Desk this morning.

Debt Desk

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk.

The first anchor is rates, and this morning’s figures are verified from the U.S. Treasury’s July 27 par yield curve close and the New York Fed’s latest official SOFR release. The curve finished Monday, July 27, at 4.31 percent on the 2-year, 4.40 percent on the 5-year, 4.65 percent on the 10-year, and 5.12 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.64 percent for July 24.

That move in Treasurys matters because it gave borrowers a little relief at the long end versus Friday without changing the larger story. The 10-year backed off to 4.65 from 4.69, and the 30-year eased to 5.12 from 5.16, but duration is still expensive enough that permanent debt is not suddenly easy. The shape of the curve is also worth paying attention to. The front end remains sticky, SOFR is still in the mid-3s, and the curve from 2s through 30s is positively sloped. That is a market saying short money is still not cheap, but longer money still demands a real premium. For borrowers, the practical implication is the same one we have been talking about: bridge and shorter-duration executions still make sense when the business plan can support them, while fixed-rate permanent debt needs a stronger conviction call than it did in lower-rate cycles.

This is why the fresh deal flow keeps pointing back to multifamily and to lenders that can live with transitional or refinance-heavy stories. Commercial Observer reported yesterday that multifamily now makes up roughly 80 percent of the collateral in a sample of recent CRE CLO deals reviewed by CRED iQ. Those deals totaled about $4.68 billion across 160 loans, and the pattern is pretty clear. Lenders and bond buyers are still willing to finance risk, but they want it in property types and structures they understand. Right now that means apartments, and very often it means full-term interest-only bridge paper.

That apartment refinance theme showed up again in CoStar’s reporting yesterday on Arbor Realty’s latest $768 million bond offering. The framing there is useful because it is not just one isolated securitization story. It is a window into how much of the multifamily market is still centered on refinancing existing debt rather than reaching for new ground-up exposure. Owners are still solving for maturity schedules, coupon shock and recapitalization needs, and lenders that can aggregate those loans into bond execution are telling you there is still deep demand for apartment credit, even if the use of proceeds is more defensive than celebratory.

CMBS is also giving a more nuanced picture than the old open-or-shut narrative. Commercial Observer reported last week that Citi priced the largest multifamily-only conduit CMBS transaction originated by a single bank since the global financial crisis, an $816.9 million deal backed by 27 five-year, interest-only loans. That is a meaningful data point. It says securitized capital is not retreating from apartments. But it also says the market wants a familiar asset class, seasoned collateral and structures that investors can underwrite quickly. On the single-asset side, Commercial Observer also reported three days ago that Nomura priced the largest sole-bank SASB CMBS deal in nearly two years. Again, the message is not that CMBS is wide open. The message is that the window is open for clean stories, strong sponsorship and assets that can carry investor confidence.

That is the right bridge into execution tone across the lender stack. Banks are more present than they were a year ago and are clearly wading back into commercial real estate, but the appetite still looks disciplined. The money is there for good apartments, strong sponsors and relationship business, yet proceeds and structure are still conservative by the standards of the easy-money era. Life companies also have allocations to put out, and industry commentary this year has pointed to spread compression on select high-quality assets, but that lane is still mostly for highly stabilized deals where leverage is modest and the cash flow story is beyond debate. In other words, life company money is real, but it is not there to rescue weak capitalization.

Debt funds remain the most flexible lane. They are still the place borrowers go when they need speed, lease-up runway, construction leverage, conversion capital or a refinancing bridge that conventional lenders will not stretch to provide. The recent CLO mix reinforces that. These lenders are still central to execution because they can solve timing and complexity, not just price risk.

CMBS sits in the middle. It can absolutely work, especially in multifamily, SASB and well-structured specialty housing deals, but it is still living with the maturity wall in the background. Trepp’s recent reporting showed the overall CMBS delinquency rate easing in June to 7.35 percent and the multifamily special servicing rate improving to 8.23 percent, which is better than where the market was earlier in the cycle. But better does not mean loose. Trepp is also still highlighting a heavy 2026 maturity pipeline, and that overhang keeps conduit underwriting selective even when the headline delinquency numbers improve.

The agency lane remains the cleanest for multifamily, especially when the affordability or stabilization story is solid. Freddie Mac’s official update effective July 13 set its new refinance test with an implied 10-year forward rate of 5.78 percent. That is a very direct reminder that even agency lenders are underwriting for a world where forward-rate risk has not disappeared. Freddie followed that with its July 20 launch of a dynamic Multi PCs pricing table, a transparency push that gives investors and lenders more current visibility into new securitizations. Fannie Mae, for its part, made its near-stabilized property submission changes effective July 20, expanding the initial pre-review requirements. That sounds procedural, but it is important because a lot of multifamily product right now sits in that almost-stabilized zone where process, documentation and lender comfort decide whether an execution is smooth or delayed.

On HUD and FHA, the signal this morning is mostly the absence of a new signal. I did not find a material new HUD multifamily policy bulletin or FHA multifamily notice published in the last 24 hours on the relevant HUD pages, so the practical read is that the FHA lane remains available but quiet. For borrowers, that usually means the hierarchy stays the same: agencies first when the collateral fits, FHA when the structure and timing justify the added process, and private credit when the transaction needs more flexibility than the public-credit channels want to offer.

The concise market snapshot this morning is this. The latest verified Treasury curve is 4.31 percent on the 2-year, 4.40 percent on the 5-year, 4.65 percent on the 10-year and 5.12 percent on the 30-year, with SOFR at 3.64 percent for July 24. Multifamily remains the deepest liquidity pocket. Debt funds are still doing the heavy lifting on transitional and refinance-heavy business. Banks and life companies are active, but selective. CMBS is working where the story is clean and the collateral is legible. Agencies still offer the best all-in execution for many apartment borrowers, but they are not waiving away rate risk.

One thing to watch is the Federal Reserve meeting that began today, Tuesday, July 28, and concludes Wednesday, July 29. Even if the Fed stands pat, the statement, press conference and market reaction could move the long end enough to change borrower behavior into month-end. If the 10-year stays closer to 4.65 and the 30-year keeps drifting off the highs, some owners may finally decide the fixed-rate window is good enough to lock. If the long end snaps back higher, expect bridge demand and refinance creativity to stay front and center.

The takeaway for Tuesday, July 28, is pretty straightforward. Nationally, the day starts with a more complicated Seattle shooting investigation, a wildfire emergency interrupting freight movement in Oregon, tariff uncertainty that is still spreading through business planning, and an oil market that has cooled but not normalized. In Debt Desk, liquidity is there, especially for multifamily, but duration is still expensive, agencies remain disciplined rather than generous, CMBS is open for the right stories, and debt funds are still essential because they can bridge the gap between what borrowers need and what the cleaner parts of the market are willing to do.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk Morning Brief for July 27, 2026
item.description: A deadly Seattle festival shooting, Trump’s tariff defense as the Gordie Howe bridge opens, and new questions over Pentagon casualty accounting lead the national brief before Debt Desk turns to Monday’s verified rate setup, fresh multifamily bridge and agency financings, CMBS execution and maturity pressure, agency and HUD developments, and one thing to watch for Monday, July 27, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
It is Monday, July 27th, and this is Debt Desk.

National

Let’s start with the morning brief, because the national backdrop for this Monday is a mix of violence in a major city gathering, trade pressure showing up in the industrial heartland, new transparency questions around the Iran conflict, and a climate story in the American West that is starting to look less like background and more like operating reality.

The first headline this morning is from Seattle, where the weekend ended with a mass shooting at the Bite of Seattle festival near the Space Needle. The Associated Press reported on July 27 that three people were killed and four others were wounded, including a 2-year-old boy. Police arrested one suspect at the scene and were still looking for a second. On its face, this is a local criminal investigation, but stories like this also shape the broader national conversation about public safety, event security and the willingness of cities to keep leaning into outdoor foot traffic and destination programming as part of downtown recovery. Seattle is not a Sun Belt growth market talking point. It is a large, visible urban market, and when something like this happens at a signature public event, it lands well beyond the city limits.

The second story is trade, and it is not abstract anymore. AP reported on July 27 that President Trump traveled to Michigan to defend his economic program while the impact of the administration’s latest tariff moves is getting harder to separate from local politics and cross-border commerce. The timing matters because traffic is set to begin on Monday, July 27, across the Gordie Howe International Bridge between Detroit and Windsor, a project that should have been a straightforward symbol of North American trade capacity. Instead, it is opening under a cloud of fresh U.S.-Canada tariff tension. For manufacturers, suppliers and logistics operators, that is the point. The physical infrastructure is improving at the same moment the policy infrastructure is getting less predictable. If you are trying to underwrite input costs, freight assumptions or capital spending tied to cross-border industrial activity, that mismatch matters.

The third story is a new layer of skepticism around the administration’s handling of the Iran conflict. AP reported on July 27 that the Pentagon’s official Iran-war casualty count no longer includes four American troops killed during renewed fighting in July. Those deaths have been moved into a new category labeled Overseas Operations, and more than 200 wounded troops also appear to have been shifted out of the main tally. That does not change what happened on the ground, but it does change the way the war is being publicly accounted for, and that is a serious issue. Congress was already uneasy about oversight, spending and mission clarity. Now the administration also has to deal with questions about whether it is presenting the public with a complete and consistent record of the costs.

The fourth story is slower moving, but it is worth your attention because it ties directly into agriculture, insurance and the economics of land in the West. AP reported on July 26 that ranchers across the Rockies are increasingly hauling water to livestock because the Upper Colorado River Basin just came through its worst snowpack on record and fast-moving wildfires are compounding the stress. That is not just a climate anecdote. It is a real-time operating cost story. When the baseline assumptions around water, forage and fire risk all shift at once, the effects work their way through ranch economics, rural credit and eventually land values. These are the kinds of stories that sit outside the daily market tape until suddenly they do not.

So that is the national frame for Monday, July 27. A deadly Seattle shooting is putting public-space security back in focus. Trade policy is colliding with a major new U.S.-Canada logistics link. The Pentagon is facing deeper scrutiny over how it counts the human cost of the Iran fight. And the drought-and-fire story in the Rockies is continuing to harden into an economic issue instead of a seasonal weather note. That is the national setup heading into Debt Desk.

Debt Desk

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk.

The first anchor is rates, and these are the verified figures from the official Treasury table and the New York Fed’s SOFR API. As of this Monday morning run on July 27, the latest Treasury close available is Friday, July 24. That curve finished at 4.33 percent on the 2-year, 4.43 percent on the 5-year, 4.69 percent on the 10-year, and 5.16 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.64 percent for July 23.

That curve still tells a very specific story about execution. The front end is not easy, but it is manageable enough that floating-rate debt remains viable for borrowers with a real business plan and a realistic takeout window. The bigger problem is duration. A 10-year just under 4.70 percent and a 30-year above 5.15 percent mean permanent money still carries a real cost, especially after spread and structure are layered on top. That is why bridge capital, shorter holds and staged refinancing strategies continue to make sense for so many borrowers. In simple terms, the market is open, but certainty is expensive.

You can hear that in the latest multifamily deal flow. Commercial Observer reported on July 24 that Lightstone Capital originated a $34.25 million bridge refinance for Kaya Apartments, a newly completed 78-unit multifamily project in San Diego’s Bankers Hill neighborhood. The project is fully leased, and that matters. This is not rescue capital for a broken story. It is bridge debt for a delivered, occupied apartment asset that still benefits from flexible execution before an owner decides whether to move into a longer-term takeout. That is a useful signpost for the market right now. Private credit is not only serving messy transitional situations. It is also serving the gap between completion and the moment when permanent financing looks compelling enough to lock.

The same article also noted that Lightstone closed another $23.4 million senior bridge loan in July for a 98-unit Carlsbad housing conversion and an $11.5 million industrial acquisition loan in Texas. The apartment angle is the important one for us. It reinforces the idea that debt funds and alternative lenders are still willing to write checks where speed, flexibility and business-plan fit matter more than absolute coupon.

Agency execution is still the cleaner lane when the collateral fits. Commercial Observer reported on July 23 that Greystone provided a $46.8 million Fannie Mae-backed refinancing for Pine Town Houses, a Section 8 garden-style apartment complex in Long Beach, New York. The loan carries a 10-year term, five years of interest-only and a 35-year amortization schedule. That is about as good an illustration as you can get of why affordable multifamily remains one of the most dependable corners of the market. When the asset has subsidy support, cash flow visibility and a clear affordability profile, the agencies can still deliver structure that many other lenders simply cannot match.

That is why the agency policy updates still matter, even when they look procedural at first glance. Fannie Mae’s Multifamily Guide shows that Guide Update 26-18 became effective on July 20 and expanded the initial pre-review submission requirements for near-stabilized properties. That may sound technical, but in this market a lot of apartment deals are not fully seasoned and not obviously unstable either. They sit in that middle zone where documentation, timing and lender confidence determine whether a borrower gets smooth execution or extra friction.

Freddie Mac is also still leaning into capital-markets transparency. On July 20, Freddie introduced a dynamic Multi PCs pricing table designed to provide weekly cover bids and high-level bond and loan details for new deals. And on its broader multifamily platform, Freddie continues to emphasize scale, including its note that as of April 30 it had surpassed a $500 billion book of business representing more than 4.7 million rental housing units nationwide. None of that changes today’s coupon, but it does reinforce the point that the agency machine is still very much running, and that matters for liquidity expectations across the multifamily market.

On the securitized side, there are two different stories running at once. The first is that specialized housing executions are still possible. Commercial Observer reported on July 23 that Systima Capital Management closed a $153 million tax-exempt private-label CMBS affordable housing transaction backed by a 1,272-unit portfolio. The deal reportedly generated more than $1.2 billion of investor orders from 19 institutional buyers. That is significant because it shows investors will still show up when the structure, collateral and mission-driven story line up.

The second CMBS story is that broad execution remains selective because the maturity wall is still staring everyone in the face. Trepp’s July commentary said the overall CMBS delinquency rate decreased 20 basis points in June to 7.35 percent, which is the headline people like to cite because it suggests improvement. But the underlying data are more nuanced. Trepp said the five largest newly delinquent loans still accounted for $998.9 million of the $2.64 billion in newly delinquent balances, and multifamily delinquencies increased 28 basis points to 7.23 percent in June. So yes, the broad delinquency rate improved, but it is not a clean all-clear signal.

Trepp’s July maturity analysis is probably the more important framing for lenders and borrowers. The firm said there are $76.6 billion of hard CMBS maturities due in 2026, with 39 percent landing in the fourth quarter, and 36 percent of those loans carrying debt yields at or below 8 percent. That is where the refinancing friction lives. It is the reason conduit lenders are willing to do deals but are still careful on leverage, asset selection and sponsor quality. The market is functioning. It just is not functioning indiscriminately.

That helps explain the current lender map. Banks are more active than they were a year ago, but they still prefer cleaner apartments, relationship borrowers and conventional stories that do not ask them to stretch on proceeds or assumptions. Life company money is still available, but mostly for highly stabilized assets where leverage stays disciplined and sponsorship is beyond debate. CMBS can absolutely work, especially in tailored or affordable-housing structures, but generic conduit execution is still governed by the refinance wall and the memory of what happens when underwriting gets too optimistic. Debt funds remain central because they can solve for timing, complexity and transitional risk in ways balance-sheet lenders often will not.

Multifamily remains the deepest lane, and recent balance-sheet data back that up. Commercial Observer reported on July 22, citing CRED iQ data, that multifamily loan balances at U.S. banks were up about 53 percent from the first quarter of 2019, the fastest growth rate among the major real estate lending categories. Multifamily balances stood at roughly $665 billion in the first quarter of 2026. That does not mean every bank wants to add apartment exposure aggressively from here. It does mean the apartment sector remains deeply embedded in the credit system, even after years of higher rates and tighter underwriting.

HUD and FHA are quieter than the agencies, but still worth tracking. HUD’s ORCF queue page was still live when checked on Monday, July 27, and there was no major new multifamily bulletin in the last 24 hours. In this market, quiet is information. It tells you the FHA lane is functioning, but it is not currently giving borrowers a new policy tailwind. For affordable and workforce housing sponsors, that usually means the practical focus stays on agency executions first, FHA where it still fits, and private credit when timing or structure pushes outside the cleanest boxes.

The concise market snapshot this morning is this. The latest verified Treasury curve is 4.33 percent on the 2-year, 4.43 percent on the 5-year, 4.69 percent on the 10-year and 5.16 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.64 percent for July 23. Debt funds are still doing a large share of the flexible apartment and transitional work. Agency execution remains the strongest outlet for affordable and well-structured multifamily. CMBS is open, especially in targeted formats, but the 2026 maturity wall is still keeping underwriting selective. And the shape of the Treasury curve still argues for shorter-duration strategies unless a borrower has a very strong reason to term out right now.

One thing to watch today is whether the long end of the curve softens at all after a weekend dominated by trade and geopolitical headlines rather than fresh inflation news. If the 10-year and 30-year stay pinned near Friday’s close, borrowers will keep favoring bridge debt, floating-rate structures and delayed permanent takeouts. If the long end eases even modestly, some sponsors may decide the window is finally good enough to lock fixed-rate proceeds instead of waiting for a cleaner setup.

The takeaway for Monday, July 27, is pretty straightforward. Nationally, the week opens with a deadly Seattle shooting, tariff politics showing up at a key U.S.-Canada trade crossing, new questions about how the Pentagon is counting the costs of the Iran fight, and a western drought story that is turning into a real economic issue. In Debt Desk, the message is that liquidity is available, but duration still costs too much, private credit remains essential, agencies still provide the cleanest multifamily execution, and CMBS is functioning best where the story is specialized and the underwriting is disciplined.
